citations.quote: Define the supersymmetry generators on $\mathscr S$ by

The supercharges $Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}$ anticommute with each $\bar D_{\dot\beta}$, so the defined supersymmetry transformation preserves chirality and induces a unique smooth component transformation.

For one generator, write a polynomial uniquely with that generator on the left as $f=f_0+\xi_i f_1$, with $f_0,f_1$ independent of $\xi_i$, and define its Berezin integral by the complex-linear coefficient-extraction rule $\int d\xi_i\,f=f_1$. Thus $\int d\xi_i\,1=0$ and $\int d\xi_i\,\xi_i=1$. Fix the ordered measures
$$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. These are formal engineering dimensions; no physical model or empirical unit convention is asserted.

derivations.claim: For any even smooth superspace function $X$, substitute the operators from [F1] into $\delta X$. Since the odd parameters are constant, the odd Leibniz rule gives $\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)$ and $-\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}X=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)$. The remaining terms are ordinary spacetime derivatives, so $\delta X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)+\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)+\partial_\mu(-i\epsilon^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}X+i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$.

For a chiral superfield $X(y,\theta)$, use $y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta$ and the left-derivative rules in [F1]–[F3]. The chain rule gives $Q_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}|_y$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}|_y+2i\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_{y^\mu}$. Since $X$ is independent of $\bar\theta$, $\delta X=\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X+2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu X$.

Expand the supercharge anticommutators from [F1]. The only nonzero terms in $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}$ are $\{\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha},i\theta^\gamma\sigma^\mu_{\gamma\dot\beta}\partial_\mu\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and $\{-i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\gamma}\bar\theta^{\dot\gamma}\partial_\mu,-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}}\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$. Terms with two odd coordinates cancel under symmetrization, and derivatives in distinct generators anticommute by [F3]. Hence $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}=2i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and both same-chirality anticommutators are zero.

Apply step 1.1 to the even D-term integrand $X=K(\bar\Phi,\Phi)$, whose finite nilpotent Taylor expansion is smooth. Each odd-coordinate derivative has zero top coefficient in the ordered Grassmann basis from [F3], so its Berezin integral vanishes. The spacetime-divergence term integrates to zero because the field-dependent part of $K$ is compactly supported and its constant exterior value has zero supersymmetry variation. Thus the D-term action is invariant.

The first term in step 1.2 integrates to zero under $d^2\theta$ by the same coefficient-extraction calculation as step 2.1. The second is the spacetime divergence $\partial_\mu(2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$; compact support removes its boundary term. Holomorphicity and chirality make $W(\Phi)$ chiral, and complex conjugation gives the same conclusion for its antichiral conjugate. Therefore the F-term action is invariant.

By [F2], the transformations preserve the chiral constraint, so the transformed field has the unique component expansion in [F1]. Coefficient extraction is linear; therefore the operator identities in step 1.3 induce the same translation algebra on every component, including the independent auxiliary field $F^i$. No Euler–Lagrange equation was used, proving off-shell closure.

derivations.claim: Since $F^i$ occurs algebraically and without derivatives, its Euler–Lagrange equation is the ordinary partial derivative of $\mathcal L_F$ with respect to the independent conjugate coordinate $\bar F^{\bar j}$. Differentiating [A1] gives $g_{i\bar j}F^i+\bar W_{\bar j}=0$.

Expand the Hermitian square $g_{i\bar j}(F^i+g^{i\bar k}\bar W_{\bar k})(\bar F^{\bar j}+g^{\ell\bar j}W_\ell)$. The two cross terms are $F^iW_i$ and $\bar F^{\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}$ because $g_{i\bar j}g^{\ell\bar j}=\delta_i^\ell$ and $g_{i\bar j}g^{i\bar k}=\delta_{\bar j}^{\bar k}$; the final term is $g^{\ell\bar k}W_\ell\bar W_{\bar k}$. Therefore $\mathcal L_F$ equals this square minus $g^{\ell\bar k}W_\ell\bar W_{\bar k}$.
Positive definiteness makes $g$ invertible. Multiply the equation in step 1.1 by $g^{k\bar j}$ and use $g^{k\bar j}g_{i\bar j}=\delta_i^k$ to obtain $F^k=-g^{k\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}$.

Substitute the solution from step 2.1: the square in step 1.2 vanishes, so the on-shell auxiliary Lagrangian is $-g^{i\bar j}W_i\bar W_{\bar j}$. The inverse of a positive-definite Hermitian matrix is positive definite, so this contraction is nonnegative; for $g_{i\bar j}=\delta_{i\bar j}$ it is $\sum_i|W_i|^2$. This is the classical scalar potential in the stated F-term sector.

citations.quote: Define the supersymmetry generators on $\mathscr S$ by

Use the selected smooth right-principal $SU(2)$ bundle $P\to M$ and its connection $A$ from the non-Abelian Yang–Mills model, with $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$, and positive dimensionless coupling $g_{\mathrm{YM}}$. For each matter representation, let $V_R$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hermitian space and $R:SU(2)\to U(V_R)$ a smooth unitary representation; write $\rho_{R*}$ for its Lie-algebra differential. In the fundamental representation set $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $t_a=iT_a=\sigma_a/2$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_2(t_at_b)=\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$. In representation $R$, set $t_{a,R}=i\rho_{R*}(T_a)$. In a local trivialization write $V=V^at_a$ and $V_R=V^at_{a,R}$, and set $A_\mu=-i g_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu$ when $B_\mu=B_\mu^at_a$ is its vector component. Thus the matter covariant derivative is $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+\rho_{R*}(A_\mu)=\partial_\mu-i g_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu^at_{a,R}$.

A **vector superfield prepotential** is a dimensionless smooth even real matrix-valued superfield $V$ in the finite Grassmann-valued superspace of the N=1 chiral-superfield convention. Under a global rigid supersymmetry variation it transforms as $\delta V=(\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha+\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha})V$, with the supercharges defined in the chiral-superfield convention. Its local gauge transformations are $\Phi_R\mapsto e^{i\Lambda_R}\Phi_R$ and $e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}\mapsto e^{i\Lambda_R^\dagger}e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}e^{-i\Lambda_R}$, where $\Phi_R$ is chiral, $V_R=V^at_{a,R}$, and $\Lambda_R=\Lambda^at_{a,R}$ is a dimensionless chiral gauge-parameter superfield in the represented complexified Lie algebra $\mathfrak{su}(2)_{\mathbb C}=\mathfrak{su}(2)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$. The associated represented matrix curvature is defined by

$$\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}=-\tfrac14\bar D^{\dot\beta}\bar D_{\dot\beta}\!\left(e^{-2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}D_\alpha e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}\right),$$

where $D_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}+i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}-i\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu$. Admissible vector-superfield data require $\bar D_{\dot\gamma}\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}=0$ and the adjoint transition law $\mathscr C_{\alpha,j}=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}\mathscr C_{\alpha,i}$ on each overlap with principal transition function $g_{ij}$.

Distinguish this represented curvature from the abstract connection-normalized Lie-algebra-valued curvature $\mathcal W_\alpha$. With canonical adjoint component field strength $W^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$, the matrix convention is $\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}=2g_{\mathrm{YM}}t_{a,R}W^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$, whereas $\mathcal W_\alpha=g_{\mathrm{YM}}T_aW^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$. Since $t_{a,R}=i\rho_{R*}(T_a)$, their precise dictionary is

$$\rho_{R*}(\mathcal W_\alpha)=\frac{\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}}{2i}.$$

In the fundamental representation this gives $\kappa_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal W^\alpha,\mathcal W_\alpha)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2(\mathscr C^\alpha\mathscr C_\alpha)$, where $\kappa_{\mathbb C}=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2$ is evaluated on the Lie-algebra matrices $\mathcal W$, not on the raw $\mathscr C$. Thus the chiral action coefficient $\kappa_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal W^\alpha,\mathcal W_\alpha)/(4g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2)$ equals $\operatorname{Tr}_2(\mathscr C^\alpha\mathscr C_\alpha)/(8g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2)$, before adding its Hermitian conjugate. This is a fixed real-coupling classical normalization identity; it is not a quantum-field rescaling or measure identity. Both curvatures are chiral and have the corresponding conjugation/transition law. The abstract $\mathcal W$ has the connection-normalized gaugino and auxiliary components specified below.

In a local Wess–Zumino-gauge representative, the canonical component fields in the prepotential are a Hermitian gauge potential $B_\mu$, an adjoint Grassmann-odd Weyl gaugino $\lambda_{B,\alpha}$, and a real adjoint auxiliary field $D_B$, with expansion $V_{\mathrm{WZ}}=\theta\sigma^\mu\bar\theta B_\mu+i\theta^2\bar\theta\bar\lambda_B-i\bar\theta^2\theta\lambda_B+\tfrac12\theta^2\bar\theta^2D_B$. Here $\theta^2=\theta^\alpha\theta_\alpha$ and $\bar\theta^2=\bar\theta_{\dot\alpha}\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$ use the fixed antisymmetric spinor tensors. Their dimensions are $[B_\mu]=1$, $[\lambda_B]=3/2$, and $[D_B]=2$. The connection-normalized fields are $A_\mu=-ig_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu$, $\lambda=g_{\mathrm{YM}}\lambda_B$, and $D=g_{\mathrm{YM}}D_B$; hence $[A_\mu]=1$, $[\lambda]=3/2$, and $[D]=2$. The full prepotential is used for supersymmetry transformations; Wess–Zumino gauge is only a component representative and need not be preserved by an uncompensated supersymmetry variation.

The supercharges $Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}$ anticommute with each $\bar D_{\dot\beta}$, so the defined supersymmetry transformation preserves chirality and induces a unique smooth component transformation.

For one generator, write a polynomial uniquely with that generator on the left as $f=f_0+\xi_i f_1$, with $f_0,f_1$ independent of $\xi_i$, and define its Berezin integral by the complex-linear coefficient-extraction rule $\int d\xi_i\,f=f_1$. Thus $\int d\xi_i\,1=0$ and $\int d\xi_i\,\xi_i=1$. Fix the ordered measures
$$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. These are formal engineering dimensions; no physical model or empirical unit convention is asserted.

derivations.claim: For an even smooth matrix-valued superspace integrand $X$, expand $\delta X$ using [F1]. The odd Leibniz rule and constancy of the parameters give $\delta X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)+\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)+\partial_\mu(-i\epsilon^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}X+i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$. The same identity holds entrywise for matrices because $Q$ acts by derivations.

The superpotential is chiral: the chain rule gives $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}W_G(\Phi)=\sum_a(\partial W_G/\partial\Phi^a)\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi^a=0$. The vector field strength is chiral by [F2]. Therefore both $W_G(\Phi)$ and $\kappa_\mathbb C(\mathcal W^\alpha,\mathcal W_\alpha)$ are chiral even superfields.

For $X=\sum_a\bar\Phi^a e^{2gV_{R_a}}\Phi^a$, the finite Grassmann expansion has smooth coefficients, and the ordinary finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth in the body coefficients; hence step 1.1 applies. The odd-coordinate derivatives have no top Grassmann coefficient by [F4], so their D-term integrals vanish. The spacetime divergence integrates to zero under the compact-support or relative-action boundary condition in [A1]. Thus every matter D-term is invariant.

For either chiral integrand $Y$ in step 1.2, change to $y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta$. By [F1] and [F3], $Q_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}|_y$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}|_y+2i\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_{y^\mu}$. Since $Y$ is independent of $\bar\theta$, $\delta Y=\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}Y+2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu Y$. The first term integrates to zero by Berezin coefficient extraction, and the second is a spacetime divergence with vanishing boundary contribution. The conjugate antichiral terms obey the conjugate identity.

The D-term and all chiral F-term variations in steps 2.1 and 2.2 integrate to zero. Their sum is the complete action in [A1], so $\delta S_{\mathrm{GM}}=0$. The argument uses only the declared superspace variation and auxiliary fields; it invokes no equations of motion, gauge fixing, or quantum construction.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

The connection-normalized fields are $A_\mu=-ig_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu$, $\lambda=g_{\mathrm{YM}}\lambda_B$, and $D=g_{\mathrm{YM}}D_B$; hence $[A_\mu]=1$, $[\lambda]=3/2$, and $[D]=2$. The full prepotential is used for supersymmetry transformations; Wess–Zumino gauge is only a component representative and need not be preserved by an uncompensated supersymmetry variation.
The matter covariant derivative is $D_\mu\phi^a=\partial_\mu\phi^a+\rho_{a*}(A_\mu)\phi^a=\partial_\mu\phi^a-ig B_\mu^b t_{b,a}\phi^a$, where $t_{b,a}=i\rho_{a*}(T_b)$ and $T_b=-i\sigma_b/2$.

derivations.claim: The fundamental matrices are $t_1=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $t_2=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $t_3=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Substituting $A_\mu=-ig_{\mathrm{YM}}\sum_aB_\mu^at_a$ into [F2] and multiplying by $(u,v)^T$ gives the two component expressions in the Example.

Write $R=R_{\mathrm f}(h)$. By [A1] and the differential of the smooth representation in [F1], $\rho_{\mathrm f*}(A_\mu')=R^{-1}\rho_{\mathrm f*}(A_\mu)R+R^{-1}\partial_\mu R$. Since differentiating $RR^{-1}=I$ gives $\partial_\mu(R^{-1})=-R^{-1}(\partial_\mu R)R^{-1}$, expand the transformed covariant derivative to obtain $D_\mu'\phi'=\partial_\mu(R^{-1}\phi)+\rho_{\mathrm f*}(A_\mu')R^{-1}\phi=R^{-1}(\partial_\mu\phi+\rho_{\mathrm f*}(A_\mu)\phi)=R^{-1}D_\mu\phi$.

Unitarity gives $(R^{-1}D_\mu\phi)^\dagger(R^{-1}D^\mu\phi)=(D_\mu\phi)^\dagger RR^{-1}D^\mu\phi=(D_\mu\phi)^\dagger D^\mu\phi$. Thus the scalar kinetic density in [F3] is independent of the chosen local frame.
